title: Bipartisan group of senators call on Trump to rescind Russian diesel deal
description: President Trump stops to speak to member
body:
President Trump stops to speak to members of the media as he departs the White House on Oct. 13, 2026.
                
                    Win McNamee/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Win McNamee/Getty Images
    

   
   A bipartisan group of senators is calling on President Trump to rescind his recent diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin, calling it a "betrayal of the people of Ukraine."    Last week, Trump announced via social media he had struck a deal with Putin, whereby Russia will supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the American and global market, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and one million tons "immediately thereafter."   "Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel," Trump wrote.    
   His announcement stunned lawmakers, who passed legislation this summer directing the president to impose significant tariffs on the top importers of Russian oil.    Those sanctions are aimed at targeting Russian officials, companies and financial institutions helping fuel Russia's war in Ukraine. The legislation was named in memory of the late GOP Sen. Lindsey Graham, who helped negotiate Trump's support for the package.   "This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our allies; it should be rescinded," wrote six Republican and six Democratic senators in a letter Tuesday to the president.   "The deal you struck with President Vladimir Putin on October 9th will not achieve just ends, nor will it benefit Americans," it read.    Senators said they recognized the need to lower energy costs for Americans — but maintained that allowing Russian diesel into global markets will offer "limited to no relief to Americans."   They added the deal "only provides Putin with more fuel to finance his war machine and enables Russia to continue its brutal attacks on Ukrainian civilians."   When asked about the letter, the White House referred back to comments President Trump made to reporters on Tuesday about concerns that Russia will use proceeds from the diesel agreement to purchase weapons.    
   "Nobody's telling me anything," Trump said. "That's a diesel deal. Not for us. That's being released into the world. That's not being released to us. That's a diesel deal that's going to be released into the world for the world market, because the world market suffered with high prices."    The letter was signed by Democrats Richard Blumenthal, Chris Coons, Dick Durbin, Jack Reed, Jeanne Shaheen and Sheldon Whitehouse. They were joined by Republicans Alan Armstrong, Susan Collins, John Cornyn, Mitch McConnell, Lisa Murkowski and Thom Tillis.

Kimberly Guilfoyle has been asked to resign among corruption allegations   Kimberly Guilfoyle has been asked to resign as US ambassador to Greece following allegations that she sought payment from a Trump donor in exchange for access to administration officials

    
        Politics
    


      
                  
            October 13, 20264:03 PM ET
         
      
   
                              By                               ,                
            


      
      Kimberly Guilfoyle has been asked to resign among corruption allegations

      Kimberly Guilfoyle has been asked to resign as US ambassador to Greece following allegations that she sought payment from a Trump donor in exchange for access to administration officials   


    
        
          Transcript
        
    SCOTT DETROW, HOST:  The White House says it has asked Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign as ambassador to Greece amid mounting reports of misconduct. NPR's Michele Kelemen reports, this comes a week after Secretary of State Marco Rubio visited with her in Athens.MICHELE KELEMEN, BYLINE: Kimberly Guilfoyle is a prominent figure in Trump's MAGA movement, a former Fox News commentator once engaged to Donald Trump Jr. Her firing was announced by the new White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)KATIE ZACHARIA: We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign.KELEMEN: President Trump played down his relationship with her, saying she dated his son a long time ago. Speaking near his new helipad, the president says he has not spoken to Guilfoyle.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: I didn't speak to her, no, but she will not be there (ph). I didn't like what I read.KELEMEN: The Wall Street Journal has been publishing numerous allegations about Guilfoyle, accepting improper gifts and offering to use her influence in the Trump administration in return for paying off her credit card bill. Secretary of State Marco Rubio sounded frustrated when reporters asked him about this during his visit last week to Athens.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)MARCO RUBIO: You guys somehow walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it's the gospel. It's not the gospel. It's not the gospel for me.KELEMEN: The State Department's inspector general's office would not comment on reports of an investigation into Guilfoyle's alleged misconduct. Guilfoyle has rejected all allegations, posting on social media that she will vigorously defend her name, reputation and integrity. Retired Ambassador Eric Rubin, who used to head the State Department's union, says this all looks bad for the United States.ERIC RUBIN: I think Europeans are snickering. I think there are people in Greece who are snickering, and that's not good for us. We should have somebody who's respected and who carries the weight of the position.KELEMEN: In the past, about 60% of America's ambassadors were career Foreign Service officers, but that's down to about 5%, as Trump names mostly political ambassadors.RUBIN: And some of it is just friends, cronies and donors. And again, it's always - we've always had some of those in every administration, but not in these numbers.KELEMEN: The ranking Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Congressman Gregory Meeks, is vowing to press for further investigations into Guilfoyle, telling NPR, quote, "serving as a U.S. ambassador is a position of public trust, not a business opportunity." Michele Kelemen, NPR News, the State Department.(SOUNDBITE OF ALEX VAUGHN SONG, "SO BE IT")

title: Trump's ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, resigns after allegations of improper conduct
description: FILE - Kimberly Guilfoyle speaks as Pres
body:
FILE - Kimberly Guilfoyle speaks as President Donald Trump listens at a reception celebrating Greek Independence Day in the East Room of the White House, March 24, 2025, in Washington.
                
                    Jacquelyn Martin/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jacquelyn Martin/AP
    

   
   WASHINGTON — The White House publicly asked for U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle's resignation on Tuesday as she faced mounting accusations of improper conduct, and she announced within two hours that she was quitting, ending days of talk and speculation about her professional fate. Guilfoyle insisted that she would "vigorously defend" herself.   
   President Donald Trump's administration had said earlier Tuesday it had asked Guilfoyle to leave her post after she faced severe criticism over allegations she engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens.   That revelation came in response to a question to freshly minted White House press secretary Katie Zacharia at her first media briefing Tuesday morning. Zacharia said Guilfoyle "has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well."   "She went to Greece. She was doing a good job, but we didn't like what we were reading," Trump said just after Guilfoyle's resignation, which was posted on her X account. He said he had not spoken to her but "she will not be there."   
   Guilfoyle's departure comes after its possibility was previewed to The Associated Press over the weekend and Trump registered his unhappiness on Monday at reports about her alleged conduct. Those comments came a day after the AP, citing a senior U.S. official, reported that Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were "extremely pissed off" by Guilfoyle's reported conduct.   Guilfoyle denies the accusations and cites her 'decades of public service'   In a series of stories dating to late last month, The Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to use her influence inside the Republican administration in return for the payment of a large credit card bill.   Guilfoyle addressed the accusations directly in her resignation post on X, saying, "These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity."   "I have dedicated my professional life to fighting for justice, standing up for what is right, and defending the values that make America exceptional," she said. "I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service."   In a statement released late Sunday, Guilfoyle's lawyers denied that she had done anything wrong and claimed that the money she was seeking from a Trump donor was payment for services — public appearances and speaking engagements that predate her ambassadorial nomination — that had not been paid.   
   The lawyers, David Schwartz and Jesse Binnall, also rejected allegations of impropriety related to Guilfoyle's travel on private planes, saying that before every such trip she "sought, obtained and followed State Department guidance and followed the Department's travel regulations."   They did not immediately return calls Tuesday.   The allegations began surfacing weeks ago   After defending Guilfoyle following the first report, Rubio declined to comment publicly on the growing allegations. Last week, Rubio said: "Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here."   But after another report appeared later, Rubio — speaking Thursday before leaving Athens — berated journalists for asking about the allegations. He said that he didn't know if they were true and that he would not respond if he could not confirm them.   "You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it's the gospel. It's not the gospel. It's not the gospel for me. That's not the way we do things," Rubio said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart, looked on.   A second U.S. official, who also spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss personnel matters, said the State Department's inspector general was looking into the allegations, which first began surfacing in the Journal late last month and have since multiplied.   The second official could not say if a formal IG probe had begun. Inspectors general often conduct informal inquiries into complaints against staffers, and many times those inquiries do not result in a full-on investigation, which can result in disciplinary action up to and including dismissal. The State Department has declined to comment on a potential IG investigation.   There was no immediate response to Zacharia's statement from the Greek government or Cabinet members.   Ahead of Tuesday's announcement, Greek opposition parties had called on the Foreign Ministry to summon Guilfoyle to respond to the allegations made against her. "This, most importantly, is an issue of national dignity," Sia Anagnostopoulou, a former deputy foreign minister, said in parliament Friday. Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis responded that Guilfoyle had been treated "the same way as every other ambassador" and argued that an official summons had not been necessary.   
   Hours earlier, Guilfoyle had posted photos of her meeting this week with the Spanish ambassador to Athens as well as birthday wishes for Lara Trump, the president's daughter-in-law, accompanied by Dua Lipa's "Dance the Night," from the 2023 soundtrack of the movie "Barbie."   Greece has taken on an increasingly important and influential role because of its geographic location in Southeastern Europe and the Eastern Mediterranean, particularly on energy issues as the war with Iran has spiked global oil prices. Besides the vast number of Greek-registered oil tankers that regularly ply the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, Greece is well positioned to be a pipeline conduit for liquefied natural gas imports into the Balkans and beyond.   As the U.S. ambassador to Greece, Guilfoyle had put an emphasis on energy issues, although her close association with executives in that sector was part of what got her into trouble.   Democrats call for an investigation   The top two Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs and Senate Foreign Relations committees, Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York and Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, as well as the ranking member on the House Committee for Oversight and Government Reform, Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., have already called for an investigation into Guilfoyle.   Since late September, the Journal has detailed numerous accounts of questionable conduct by Guilfoyle. Its first report said that she had told guests at a reception that the United States could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings.   While Rubio was in Athens, the Journal reported — citing text messages — that Guilfoyle had asked a Trump donor and supporter to pay a $100,000 credit card bill just before her confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials if he did.   
   The Journal then reported that Guilfoyle had been enraged about not being invited to a Greek-themed event at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, earlier this year and demanded to attend while boasting about luxury travel to France with energy company executives.   Another report, from the British tabloid The Daily Mail, said that Guilfoyle had alienated staff at the U.S. Embassy in Athens and had pushed the bounds of behavior appropriate for the top representative of the U.S. government to Greece.   Guilfoyle is a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was married to Democrat Gavin Newsom when he was San Francisco's mayor, before he became California's governor. She later was engaged to Trump's son Donald Trump Jr.

title: Why does Pete Hegseth want to livestream an execution?
description: Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has proposed livestreaming the execution of a man convicted of the 2009 attack on Fort Hood. Some scholars sa
body:
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has proposed livestreaming the execution of a man convicted of the 2009 attack on Fort Hood. Some scholars say the idea is rooted in his religious background.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    AILSA CHANG, HOST:  It has been 90 years since the U.S. government publicly executed someone. Since then, the idea of public executions in the U.S. has largely been forgotten. But last week, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced that the Pentagon would livestream the execution of the man convicted in the 2009 attack on Fort Hood. And some religious scholars see this proposal as one rooted in Hegseth's particular brand of Christian nationalism. NPR domestic extremism correspondent Odette Yousef joins us now to discuss. Hi, Odette.ODETTE YOUSEF, BYLINE: Hey, Ailsa.CHANG: Hey. OK, so let's just back up a bit. Can you please remind everyone about what happened in the attack on Fort Hood 17 years ago?YOUSEF: Sure. So on November 5 of 2009, a U.S. Army major named Nidal Hasan killed 13 people and injured another 32 in what's since been called the worst terrorist attack on U.S. soil since September 11, 2001. Now, Hasan was an Army psychiatrist who was radicalized into violent Islamist extremism. And after the attack, Ailsa, investigations found that there were numerous failures over the course of his time in the military. Peers and superiors were aware of his radicalization, but there was no meaningful action taken to discipline or remove him.CHANG: And now he may be the first American to be publicly executed by the federal government in - what? - nearly a century. How is the Pentagon explaining this decision?YOUSEF: Well, Hegseth talks about this as a deterrent to possible future similar attacks. But I spoke with Julie Ingersoll about this. She's a professor of religious studies at the University of North Florida, and she's an expert on the church that Hegseth belongs to, called the Communion of Reformed Evangelical Churches. And Ingersoll told me that when she heard about this public execution by firing squad, her thoughts immediately went to Hegseth's religious background.JULIE INGERSOLL: Part of their theology is the dominion mandate, so building a theocracy is a religious act for them. And executing infidels is part of that theocratic vision.CHANG: Wow. Just those words like infidels, theocratic vision. Can you just help us understand why she's using words like that there?YOUSEF: Yeah. So, you know, within certain strands of Christian nationalism, including the CREC, there is a belief that they have a mandate to impose their interpretation of Christianity over all aspects of life. So, Ailsa, they speak of building God's dominion on Earth. You know, some people use the word theocracy when they describe this project. You know, the more technically correct term may be theonomy, meaning, you know, government by God or subject to God's authority.As for the term infidels here, this refers to Hegseth particular apparent animus toward Islam. You know, Hegseth has tattoos valorizing the medieval crusades. One of his books is titled "American Crusade," and he's written critically about increases in Muslim populations in England and in the U.S. So all of this, you know, paired with a pretty unanimous support for the death penalty within the church that Hegseth belongs to, you know, that's how you get this proposal to livestream an execution.CHANG: But there are still questions about whether this public execution will actually happen, right? Because Vice President JD Vance expressed his discomfort with this whole idea just last week. And if this doesn't go forward, do you see the discussion around public execution going away anytime soon?YOUSEF: So, you know, this is, I think, what's particularly concerning to Ingersoll, as well as Matthew Taylor (ph), another religious expert I spoke to. Both of them told me that, in some ways, the damage is already done just by the public proposal of this method of justice. And that's because, you know, an idea that lies at the very extreme end of what the public considers acceptable policy has now been put forth by a powerful Cabinet member.CHANG: Right.YOUSEF: And so just that itself shifts the boundaries of the conversation. You know, what was once unthinkable, unsayable, has been said. And so people are now considering this. And that is how, you know, more generally, Ailsa, we see extremist ideas shift the public conversation.CHANG: That is NPR domestic extremism correspondent Odette Yousef. Thank you, Odette.YOUSEF: Thanks for having me.

title: A judge blocks the government's tree-clearing spree at a municipal D.C. golf course
description: The Trump administration abruptly cut do
body:
The Trump administration abruptly cut down more than 400 trees at Washington, D.C.'s historic East Potomac Golf Links last weekend. A federal judge has ordered testimony from two high-level officials with the Interior Department; the judge plans to hold another hearing Oct. 19.
                
                    Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR
    

   
   A federal judge has temporarily barred the Trump administration from cutting down additional trees at a D.C. municipal golf course, the latest example of a court intervening in the government's efforts to reshape pieces of the nation's capital.   The long-simmering fight over East Potomac Golf Links — which President Trump wants to redevelop into a championship-level course — erupted over the weekend, after the administration cut down hundreds of trees with little notice.   U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes had ordered the administration in May to get court approval before cutting down more than 10 trees at the golf course. Officials notified the court just before 5 p.m. on Friday of their plan to remove "up to 529 trees" in phases starting on Saturday — and had razed at least 430 by the end of the day, prompting Reyes to call an emergency hearing on Monday.   
   "What has happened has cost the government all of its credibility with me in this case," Reyes said during the nearly four-hour hearing, held via videoconference.   Reyes ordered a short-term stop to the tree-clearings, which she extended on Tuesday through Oct. 26. She warned Monday that "if that order is violated by two seconds, there are going to be contempt proceedings."   Reyes also ordered top officials from the Department of Interior and the National Park Service to testify at a hearing next Monday, to shed more light on the government's motivations and the future of the historic course.   "The questions go to whether or not I've been lied to," Reyes said. "Whether I've been lied to in declarations about the plans, whether or not I've been lied to about the timing of things, and whether I've been lied to about what kind of notice the court was going to receive."   East Potomac has emerged as another flashpoint in Trump's unilateral quest to remake D.C., and it's the subject of a lawsuit by critics who fear it could go the way of the now-lost White House East Wing unless a court intervenes. The D.C. Preservation League, along with two concerned residents, sued the government in February over what it calls an unlawful takeover.   
   "This is a tactic we're seen before from the Trump-Vance administration – act quickly to irrevocably alter a cherished national landmark, just to advance another one of President Trump's pet vanity projects," Skye Perryman, president and CEO of Democracy Forward — one of the firms involved in the lawsuit — said in a statement this weekend.   Perryman told NPR on Tuesday that the golf course is the latest in a pattern of the Trump administration "undermining the entire checks and balances process in this country, which includes undermining court proceedings."   Trump has long floated the idea of redeveloping East Potomac into a championship-caliber course and announced plans to do so earlier this year, though his target Sept. 1 start date has come and gone without a formal proposal.   The prospect — and the lack of clarity since — has raised alarm among locals concerned about losing access to the historically affordable course and to the surrounding recreational area, which is popular with cyclists, runners, fishers and picnickers.    Loading... 
   "This is a broader story than just about golf, especially when there's been this little transparency, … to say, 'Here's what the future of this little man-made peninsula is actually going to look like,'" Alex Rosen, a D.C.-based consultant who started the nonprofit Save East Po, told NPR in July.   A National Park Service official said in a Friday court filing that plans for renovations "remain in the conceptual stage." And the Interior Department told NPR in a statement on Tuesday that it is "committed to continuing the relationships we have built with the local golf communities to ensure these courses are safe, beautiful, open, affordable, enjoyable, accessible, and world-class."   But critics are growing increasingly concerned about the process itself. They worry the Trump administration is using so-called routine maintenance as a pretext to begin redevelopment without the proper authorization.   "You can't continuously say, 'There's no plan' … while you're clearly taking steps to effect a plan," Rosen, who is not involved in the lawsuit, told NPR after watching the hearing. "It's just frankly lying."   
   Why the rush? The court hopes for answers next week    At Monday's hearing, Reyes expressed regret that she hadn't issued a formal restraining order earlier, which she said was because "I have done everything humanly possible to give the government the benefit of the doubt in this case."   For example, after the administration quietly removed what it has since said were roughly 150 dying and invasive trees in late August, Reyes acknowledged that people were upset but declined to intervene: "I am not the Lorax," she said at an early September hearing.   By Monday, that benefit of the doubt was gone. When a government lawyer said they had done their best to notify the court, Reyes offered a sharp rebuke.   "You did not do your best," she said, voice raised. "You did your absolute worst."   
   Perryman, of Democracy Forward, said, "What was really remarkable about the hearing yesterday is that the government did not appear to have a defense for its failure to notify the court."   In Friday's court filing, National Mall and Memorial Parks Superintendent Kevin Griess described the tree-clearing as part of an effort "to address deferred maintenance needs and implement treatment recommendations to restore the cultural landscape."   Griess specifically cited a 2019 National Park Service report about D.C. municipal golf courses, which says several waves of tree planting at East Potomac over the last century have obscured views and changed the feel of the course from its original 1920s "links-style" design.   Griess said in his filing that NPS was able to act on the report because it had received a temporary surge of "approximately 20 to 50 trained personnel capable of performing labor-intensive grounds maintenance activities." Under questioning in court, he confirmed that surge was connected to the administration's 250th anniversary events, including the IndyCar race on the National Mall in August.   
   But critics are skeptical, given the president's public statements. Alex Dickson, one of the plaintiffs, said in a statement that "the administration is using a preservation report as cover to begin tearing out the course it was written to save."   Griess said he had gotten the green light last week from Frank Lands, the park service's deputy director of operations. At the judge's request, Lands then joined the hearing from his car in a parking lot. He said he had gotten the directive from Greg Wischer, deputy chief of staff to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum.   
   Wischer was not reachable to join the hearing, despite Reyes' request that he do so. She has ordered Wischer and Jessica Bowron, the acting director of the National Park Service, to testify at another hearing next Monday.   The Interior Department didn't answer NPR's questions about the timeline and resources for the tree-clearing, but said in a statement that "President Donald J. Trump is fulfilling his commitment to make D.C. Safe and Beautiful as shown by the working fountains, clean parks and safe streets across the district for the first time in decades."   In granting the plaintiffs' request for an extended restraining order on Tuesday, Reyes wrote that they had "proven they will likely suffer irreparable harm absent injunctive relief." She also said the government must provide "three business days' written advance notice prior to making any irreparable modification" to the golf course.

title: Civil rights advocates plan to send thousands of observers to midterm polling places
description: A voting center is seen in Scottsdale, A
body:
A voting center is seen in Scottsdale, Ariz., on Oct. 7, the first day of early voting.
                
                    Olivier Touron/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Olivier Touron/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   It was loteria night at the offices of Living United for Change in Arizona, or LUCHA, in Phoenix.   A small group of young people were playing this bingo-like card game in the hopes of taking home an array of prizes: a camping chair, reusable water bottles and coolers.   Conveniently, the prizes would be useful if you plan to camp out somewhere for a while. Which happens to be what these players were getting trained to do last week.   LUCHA, a left-of-center community organizing group, has been training volunteers to be what they call "constitutional observers" ahead of this year's midterms. This was the first of many in-person sessions the organization plans to hold as Election Day nears.   
   Carime Rodriguez, who led the training, told volunteers that their main job will be to just observe.   "Monitor the polling environment," she said. "Stay aware of what's happening on the ground … just make sure you are kind of keeping your eyes open."   For many election cycles, groups have fanned out to monitor polling places, but the charged midterm environment has many organizations stepping up efforts. They plan to have thousands of individuals with eyes on this election.   Fears of ICE at the polls   For LUCHA's Rodriguez, immigration is a concern. She told her training volunteers that during Arizona's primaries earlier this year, there was an uptick in immigration enforcement — including around polling sites in Maricopa County, where Phoenix is located.   And in case this happens again, LUCHA and other similar groups want to have people on the ground, to keep an eye out for anything they think could intimidate voters. Chiefly, groups say they are worried about Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, agents at election sites.   "I feel like these last two years, everyone has been holding on by the edge of their seats," said Alejandra Gomez, LUCHA's executive director. "And so that has made us incredibly forward thinking and making sure that we are preparing. We're hoping for the best, preparing for the worst."   
   It would be illegal for the Trump administration to send armed agents to polling sites. And administration officials have said ICE has no plans to target polling locations. But right-wing political figures close to Trump like Steven Bannon have been calling for the president to send them anyway, and Trump officials have said ICE could serve warrants at polling places.   Mary Corcoran, co-founder and executive director of the left-leaning Save America Movement, said that's enough for her to take this potential threat seriously.   "The point is to scare people and use fear as an intimidation factor to keep people home," she told NPR. "So, our perspective was that the way that we could make a difference in this election was working in communities that would be most likely impacted by the threat of ICE coming to the polls this fall."   Corcoran's group is partnering with the Rev. Al Sharpton's National Action Network, as well as various unions, like the American Federation of Teachers, in an effort they are calling Vote Safe.   She said members of the effort plan to be in major population centers with large and growing Black, Latino, Asian and immigrant populations — particularly in states with key Senate races, like Ohio, North Carolina, Georgia and Michigan.   "The volunteers are not there to engage with any ICE folks that could show up," she said. "It's really about having a de-escalatory impact by way of really bearing witness."   She said the presence of clergy, veterans, teachers and nurses from the community will hopefully have a "de-escalatory impact and a deterrent impact."   DOJ election observers   Left-leaning groups won't be the only folks at the polls. The Republican National Committee, for one, recruits observers to keep elections secure and transparent. And leaders of the Justice Department, which regularly monitors polling places, say they plan to step up their usual presence.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Harmeet Dhillon speaks to reporters on Capitol Hill on May 29.
                
                    Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
    

   
   Harmeet Dhillon, the head of DOJ's Civil Rights Division, said on Real America's Voice that she plans to send a thousand people from the agency to monitor polling sites.   
   "This is going to be the biggest DOJ election observer effort in history," she said. "And I'm so excited to be leading that effort."   She said that DOJ staff will play a similar role to other observers that will be at the polls, which is just to watch.   "They're not going to be interfering in any way or running the election, they're going to be observing, making notes," she said.   Wyoming's Republican governor criticized the actions of DOJ observers in the state in August.   "Not normal times"   Tammy Patrick with the National Association of Election Officials says election administrators have been hearing of big plans of large groups of observers for a while now. But Patrick said it's important to note that this is something they hear most election cycles.   "Every two years it seems, for at least the 20 or so years I've been doing this, we hear that there's going to be massive observation, and thousands of people are going to show up to observe at the polling place," she said.   "It hasn't manifested in that way in the past, but these are not normal times."   
   Which is why she says election administrators are educating the public. Rules about who can observe what, or how close you can be to a polling site, for example, vary from state to state.   Also, there is only so much observers can actually do at the polls. If something goes wrong, it's up to election workers and local law enforcement to sort it out.   Patrick said most years many observers get bored and leave.   "The actual process tends to be ... pretty dry," she said. "And one might even say boring to watch people walk in, give their name, sign their name, get their ballot."   But if things are not boring, Jane Kleeb with the Association of State Democratic Committees — which is part of the Democratic National Committee — said she wants people on the ground recording.   
   For political parties, the stakes of problems at the polls are high — particularly in close elections, where lawsuits are common.   "We're going to record any bad behavior," she said. "So that might be on audio. It may be still pictures, and it will be video that will then be sent to each state party. So, then they can get that information up to the DNC. So, we have a very clear process to make sure that we're documenting all of this in case lawsuits have to be filed."

schema.headline: Civil rights advocates plan to send thousands of observers to midterm polling places

title: In Kansas, a newly competitive Senate race tests limit of Trump's unpopular policies
description: A sign seen on a Kansas GOP bus tour acr
body:
A sign seen on a Kansas GOP bus tour across the state to bolster Republican candidates in an unusually competitive year. Kansas has a Democratic governor and Republican U.S. Senators but recent polls show voters could elect a Republican governor and Democratic U.S. Senator this year.
                
                    Stephen Fowler/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Stephen Fowler/NPR
    

   
   📲 Get the latest on the midterms & more in the NPR App      DODGE CITY, Kan. — If ever there were a place to symbolize both opportunities and obstacles that Democrats and Republicans face politically this midterm election, it would be Kansas.   Two years after President Trump earned 57% of the vote, Kansas Republicans are grappling with the possibility that a Democrat could win a U.S. Senate race for the first time in nearly a century.   Adam Hamilton, a self-billed "independent-minded Democrat," has led in several polls against Republican Sen. Roger Marshall.   Both parties have redirected tens of millions of dollars in recent weeks to try and shape the surprising toss-up race. The president announced Tuesday he would campaign in Wichita next week for Marshall and other Republicans on the ticket.   
   But after eight years of Democratic governor Laura Kelly who is term-limited, Republicans are also hoping to retake control of the state's top office as one of the few pickup opportunities in an otherwise daunting midterm environment.   State Senate President Ty Masterson, the Republican candidate, leads in polls against Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher in a race that is less nationalized than other competitive gubernatorial races around the country.   The last-minute shift in national attention to the Sunflower State is reflective of how unpopular Trump's second term agenda has become with voters, especially in typically Republican states in the Midwest that have been disproportionately affected by rising fuel prices and tariffs.   As early voting gets underway in Kansas, neither side is taking the voters for granted.   'It's about decency'   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Kansas Democratic Senate nominee Adam Hamilton speaks with voters in Lawrence, Kan. Monday, Oct. 12, 2026.
                
                    Stephen Fowler/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Stephen Fowler/NPR
    

   
   At a get-out-the-vote event in Lawrence Monday, Hamilton told the crowd that his priorities if elected are tackling affordability and health care, but also restoring "human decency" to politics.   "Now listen, I had somebody say to me, 'Look, I don't want somebody who's going to build bridges, I want somebody who's going to crush the Republicans,'" he said. "But here's the thing: if you want that in a state with only 25% of the population who are Democrats, you'll never get them elected.   
   "And if you did, they become part of the problem instead of part of the solution."   Hamilton is the founding pastor of Church of the Resurrection, the country's largest United Methodist Church congregation across its multiple campuses, and positions himself as a moderate voice seeking to tame rabid partisanship that has dominated modern politics.   "We've got to find solutions that will be a compromise between what the Republicans want and the Democrats want, but are going to end up getting something done as opposed to right now, where that doesn't happen very often," he said.   At a time when the Democratic Party brand is unpopular with voters, too, Hamilton is quick to point out that he's not a Democrat you might find in a blue state.   "We've been trying to make clear in our commercials that a Kansas Democrat is a bit different than a New York Democrat or a Los Angeles Democrat, and not just a little — a lot different," Hamilton told NPR.   
   That's also reflected in the slew of endorsements from conservatives, including former Republican Kansas governors Mike Hayden and Bill Graves.    Hamilton also told NPR of a recent event where Republican Party leaders said they were crossing over to vote for him.   "There were Republicans who were saying, 'We've got to do better,'" he said. "You represent our values. You represent the character we're looking for in somebody in leadership. And we know you're going to fight for both Republicans and Democrats. And they're exactly right."   Most of his stump speeches wrap with a callback to "The Wizard of Oz," with Hamilton saying Washington needs more senators "who have a brain and use it, who have a heart and feel empathy with it, and who have courage and speak up because of it."   Hamilton's campaign is also bolstered by backlash to many elements of President Trump's second term, including tariff policies and rising fuel prices, that have proven unpopular, causing the Republican Party's favorability ratings to plummet.   
   A Republican contrast to lead the state   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Kansas Republican Sen. Roger Marshall speaks to supporters at a campaign stop in Newton, Kan. President Trump is coming to campaign for Marshall and other nominees in Wichita next week.
                
                    Stephen Fowler/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Stephen Fowler/NPR
    

   
   Even as Republicans sweat the closer-than-expected Senate race, the party is optimistic about winning back control of the governor's office after eight years of Democrat Laura Kelly's leadership.   The Kansas Republican Party is on a weeklong bus tour across the state, bringing a message of contrast that is more state-focused than dealing with the challenging national environment for the party.   Masterson, the Republican gubernatorial nominee, said in Dodge City that tackling issues like affordability and lower energy prices would come from putting a Republican back in the state's top office.   "There's never been a clearer choice than we've had in this election," he said. "If you want working families to be able to afford to live, if you want to stop taxing people out of their homes and out of their businesses and off their farms, if you want safe communities, lower energy prices, i.e. then lower grocery prices… It's not really a choice. You need to vote Republican."    
   On the trail, the nominees pointed to Kelly's frequent vetoes of measures from the Republican supermajority in the legislature — and overrides of those vetoes — as a motivating factor to get voters to the polls.   State Rep. Pat Proctor, the Republican nominee for Secretary of State, said aside from the state's history of alternating support for governors from both parties, there is strong precedent for still supporting Republicans.   "We are closer to where Kansans are on all the individual issues," he said. "And when they hear us talk and they look at what we actually do, we're just closer to where they want Kansas to be."   While Republicans in other states may have to deal more with Trump's shadow over their own campaigns, campaign speeches rarely mentioned the president or his unpopular policies. Instead, it was all about painting the Democratic nominees as extreme and out of touch.   
   For his part, Marshall has painted Hamilton as too liberal, saying he would destroy Kansas' cattle, agriculture, oil and gas industries if elected.   "Kansans need to know that my opponent, Adam Hamilton, is the most radical liberal person that ever got through a primary in the state of Kansas," he said to cheers.   Still, Marshall has been dogged by negative headlines over the last month, starting with a debate at the Kansas State Fair where the senator was shouted down by the crowd repeatedly.    Marshall's campaign also faced pushback after releasing an attack ad that claimed Hamilton "protected a pedophile" used images of two unrelated businesses, and paid an outstanding invoice from a cookie shop after a viral social media post claimed the campaign failed to pay for six years.    
   Kansas is one of only a few states that currently have a senator from one party and a governor from the other party, and is one of nearly ten states where voters could also split their choices for those key positions next month.

schema.headline: In Kansas, a newly competitive Senate race tests limit of Trump's unpopular policies

title: Conservative super-lawyer squares up for his latest Supreme Court argument
body:
Attorney Paul Clement answers questions outside the U.S. Supreme Court after oral arguments in April 2022 in Washington, D.C.
                
                    Win McNamee/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Win McNamee/Getty Images
    

   
   It's arguable whether Paul Clement is the best Supreme Court advocate of his generation. But there's no doubt he's the most prolific.   When he approaches the lectern at the Supreme Court Wednesday, it will mark his 129th time arguing before the justices.   He defined the job this way at a recent conference sponsored by the conservative National Review magazine: "I always think a good working definition of a good Supreme Court advocate is somebody who's trying to get to five for their client," Clement said.   Five of nine justices — in other words, victory.   The Republican super-lawyer has racked up dozens of those wins since his days as solicitor general in the George W. Bush era.   
   For the last couple decades, Clement has worked outside government, often challenging actions by the White House. But Clement told the National Review he's still a fan of a strong executive branch.   "I'm a big believer in the unitary executive — but that doesn't mean that the president gets to do anything he wants," he said.   Clement famously tried to get the Supreme Court to overturn President Obama's signature health care law, a loss that still stings.   But he did convince the justices to deliver on other, long-held Republican priorities, like keeping judges out of partisan gerrymandering; telling courts they do not have to defer to federal agency expertise; and striking down restrictions on guns.   
   That work defending gun rights has been controversial, as his law partner Erin Murphy recalled recently.   "We had lots of different cases and clients, and over time, it just became something more and more people were complaining about," Murphy explained in  a webinar about defending unpopular clients sponsored by the conservative Federalist Society.   "The firm said you can remain at the firm only if you drop your existing clients and discontinue the Second Amendment work you had done," Murphy recalled. "We said, 'No thank you' and went and started our firm, Clement and Murphy."   
   Defending law firms against Trump orders   Ironically, Clement and Murphy are now working on behalf of big law firms, which are challenging punitive executive orders by President Trump.   Trump went after the firms for hiring attorneys who once investigated him, yanking their security clearances and barring them from federal buildings.    Clement made his case to the D.C. Circuit appeals court in May.   "The executive orders run afoul of the better part of the bill of rights," he said.   Clement argued the president violated the First Amendment rights of the law firm and had unlawfully retaliated against them.   
   "Lawyers cannot zealously represent their clients while walking on eggshells for fear of reprisals," he said. "Thus the executive orders strike at the heart of the rule of law and the zealous representation on which the judiciary and the adversary process depend."   But when Clement told the three-judge panel that he backed a strong executive branch, conservative Judge Neomi Rao, a Trump appointee, interjected.   "You know, look, I'm kind of a unitary executive guy myself, so I'm not going to tell you that a president does everything that the process ..." Clement began.   "Not any more," Rao replied, prompting murmurs from the audience. "Not any more."   "No, I really I am, I really am, trust me on that," Clement responded.   The appeals court has not yet ruled in the law firm case.   Victories against Trump administration   But Clement has already prevailed in other high-profile disputes against the Trump administration, in cases where he says they've gone too far.   For example, this year, the high court refused to allow the president to fire Lisa Cook, a member of the Federal Reserve Board.    Clement successfully defended the federal district court in Maryland, where the Trump Justice Department sued every single judge over an order on immigration detention.    
   Clement, 60, appeared on a shortlist for the Supreme Court during Trump's 2020 campaign. Given his work on behalf of several Trump targets, that idea now seems out of the question.   He told the National Review he never planned to take his foot off the gas pedal when he saw examples of overreach by the executive branch, no matter who controls the White House.   But the case he's set to argue Wednesday is one that doesn't concern the White House: it involves a 1988 law Congress passed to protect consumers' privacy when they rented videos. Clement argued in court papers that plaintiff lawyers have been stretching that old law in recent years to cover situations that extend far beyond a trip to the old Blockbuster video store.

schema.headline: Conservative super-lawyer squares up for his latest Supreme Court argument
